records.text:
### Postgres Pricing Overview

Pricing models vary fundamentally across the three platforms: **Neon** uses serverless, auto-scaling usage billing [1]; **Supabase** charges via tiered subscriptions with resource quotas [2]; and **Amazon RDS** charges provisioned rates per instance-hour and storage tier [3].

| Provider | Entry Cost | Compute Model | Storage Model | Best For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Neon** | Free tier; Launch plan has no monthly minimum [1] | Usage-based auto-scaling (billed per active compute hour) [1] | Billed per GB-month of active data & branching [1] | Variable workloads, instant branching, scale-to-zero |
| **Supabase** | Free tier; Pro starts at **$25/month** [2] | Flat monthly tier with base compute; upgradeable compute instances [2] | Included storage quota per plan; overages billed per GB [2] | Full-stack apps needing built-in Auth, Storage, and Realtime APIs alongside Postgres |
| **Amazon RDS** | AWS 12-mo Free Tier (micro instances); On-Demand hourly standard rates [3] | Provisioned hourly rates based on instance size (e.g., `db.t4g`, `db.m6g`) [3] | Provisioned storage (e.g., gp3 per GB-month) + IOPS/throughput costs [3] | Enterprise workloads requiring fine-grained control, reserved pricing, and AWS ecosystem integration |

### Deciding Factors

* **Neon:** Ideal if you want serverless compute that automatically scales up under load and scales to zero when idle, avoiding fixed instance costs [1].
* **Supabase:** Ideal if you need an all-in-one backend platform (Firebase alternative) built on top of Postgres with a predictable $25/month base rate [2].
* **Amazon RDS:** Ideal for traditional provisioned database instances, high-IOPS enterprise databases, or heavy integration into existing AWS infrastructure [3].

records.text:
The **CAP theorem** (also known as Brewer's theorem) states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of the following three guarantees:

1. **Consistency (C):** Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the exact same data at the same time.
2. **Availability (A):** Every non-failing node returns a non-error response for every request, though it cannot guarantee the response contains the latest write.
3. **Partition Tolerance (P):** The system continues to operate despite network delays, dropped messages, or loss of communication between nodes.

### The Core Trade-off
Because network partitions (**P**) are an unavoidable reality in distributed systems, the theorem effectively means that when a partition occurs, you must choose between:

* **Consistency over Availability (CP):** The system rejects or delays requests to prevent returning stale or conflicting data across separated nodes.
* **Availability over Consistency (AP):** Nodes remain open to reads and writes, but risk returning out-of-date or conflicting data until the network heals.
